Even if the function of consciousness were established in the absence of its object, such that one were to allow that the activity of "consciousness-only" could be established even when objects are non-existent during the waking state—would this not perfectly accord with the doctrine of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*)?
What is there that the proponents of the non-existence of external objects (nirālambanavādin) would not love?

If you say there is a distinct underlying intention such that all instances of contact and so forth depend upon external things to accomplish their function, yet the principle of "consciousness-only" cannot be established—just as when sandalwood is ground into fragrant paste and applied to the body, it can remove heat and distress and bring about refreshing coolness.

However, this emission arises solely based on consciousness; yet this still does not accord precisely with reason, for it is not accepted that it has an operative function based upon objects such as contact (sparśa).
This is because, while not denying the existence of external contact, one intends for others to rely upon this matter of contact to initiate activity.
Consequently, if one were to deny activity to another, it would result in the fallacy of its non-existence.
The reason for establishing that there is only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*) is that all the various functional activities of things arise from the locus of consciousness.
Regarding this, one might initially raise the following objection:
"If external objects do not exist, how can there be functional activity apart from consciousness to bring about the accomplishment of tasks?"
Since these evidences exist, I shall now set forth elegant analogies.

Just as an act of harm accomplished within a dream can produce an effect, so too can it function within consciousness-only; this has already been explained in considerable detail as previously stated.

If that were so, eating poison in a dream and the like should result in physical illness; however, this too occurs because consciousness alone possesses causal efficacy, just as there is a fixed correspondence with respect to external objects.

One may use the subsequent answer to resolve the prior doubt, or alternatively, there are times when one perceives such things as poison where, despite the absence of a real object, functional efficacy nonetheless exists.
Although it was seen that he was not bitten by the snake, the poison of doubt was able to cause him to faint, perspire, and lose his mental clarity.
Yet, had he been bitten by the snake, through the superior power of mantras, deities, and so forth, even in a dream, it would have caused him to eat his fill and become full of strength.
Furthermore, one hears of those who, seeking offspring, lie hidden upon their beds and dream of engaging in sexual union with someone, thereby obtaining a son.
How can it be known that the injuries caused by poison and the like within such a dream are non-existent?
Because one does not perceive them after waking, what is now being discussed is similar to that case:

while in the state of present awareness, one regards things as real entities and perceives poisons and the like as non-erroneous; yet when awakened by true knowledge, they are no longer seen. Thus, like those objects in a dream, their substance is not real.

However, for those who assert that real matter exists within a dream, they too would encounter such undesirable events, and the causal efficacy of poisons and the like would consequently become truly existent.

If one says they do not exist, then while there is merely the appearance of poison, the functions of poison and so forth are absent; thus, the claim regarding the "form of poison" becomes contradictory and subversive.

Granting that things such as poison and so forth are indeed established as useless because the substance of the medicine does not exist within that consciousness, one must therefore certainly know that external objects do not truly exist; rather, they merely exercise their functions upon the arising of the cognitive mind.
Just as it is in a dream, so it is upon awakening; this indeed truly accords with the principle of reality.
Thus far, we have followed the matters as they were explained, employing the separate analogy of a dream and the separate examples of ghosts and so forth.

Having already provided analogies for each of the four difficulties as they were presented, I shall now further respond to those various challenges by means of the analogy of Naraka; thus, the matter will be well established.
Due to extremely evil intentions and extremely cruel executioners, although their locations are fixed, they are not seen at all times; none of them exist as distinct forms apart from consciousness.
Furthermore, the fierce and intense suffering produced by dogs, crows, and others—corresponding to the acts of beating and torture—is experienced until the end of the retribution for one's offenses.
One may raise objections against this analogy according to its literal phrasing; all such explanations and responses should be considered as above.

Furthermore, in reality, there are no such things as extremely wicked executioners and the like. As for the matters described, some are determinate and some are indeterminate—by what cause could they arise?
Nevertheless, the mind that functions toward those objects serves as the cause for their arising at that time, because it has attained birth.

Thus, the many diverse aspects of the perceived object depend upon functional efficacy; furthermore, with the internal mental continuum’s evolving karmic force acting as the primary cause, and by additionally relying on the cooperative assistance of favorable conditions such as grasping (*upādāna*), perceptions and so forth arise according to the specific circumstances and transform, whereby the results of maturation (*vipāka*) and the like are all fully manifested.

Therefore, although there are no truly existent hell-wardens, within that realm one necessarily relies upon the predominant force of one's own previously committed similar evil karma; thus, together with others, one perceives a fixed location and so forth, and likewise gives rise to a mind that functions toward them. These very factors demonstrate that those forms and other objects are not externally real entities, but rather manifest from consciousness. This proof is formulated in order to clarify this meaning.
However, because [the cognition] does not depend on an object external to consciousness and is therefore all-pervasive, it avoids the fault of contradiction.
If objects such as tangibility were of the nature of form (*rūpa*), they would be identical to that which is being established [as the probandum].

If one says that it is merely a real entity and insists that it constitutes a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established), this should be understood as a means of exposing that fault, thereby manifesting the characteristics of the establishment of one's own position.
The reason established therein as being concordant is that consciousnesses such as dreams serve as its analogies.

This very statement of the position clarifies this meaning: because the entities existing at a specific place and time appear as various mental images to the subjective mind, just as when one’s mind is entirely obscured within a dream.

After waking from the dream, when one perceives forms and other objects with clear cognition, one is in fact not apprehending forms that are not consciousness; it is not strictly necessary for the objects such as forms to be externally manifest.
However, when things are experienced as a common enjoyment produced by the maturation of similar karma, they arise within one's own continuum without being restricted to a single individual.

This is like the various hungry ghosts who, due to their shared evil karma, perceive a river of pus and the like; or again, like those in an extremely terrible place who all see fierce executioners. In this regard, both [the object and the perception] should be established as real, for they manifest with functional efficacy just like objects perceived in the present.
Just as in a dream there is only the appearance of consciousness, wherein one sees oneself engaging in sexual intercourse with a woman;

and just as the tortures inflicted by hell-wardens and the like are witnessed by all and can be described—how could it not be necessary that these extremely wicked wardens and others first be established as non-existent before they can be used as a probans?
Since this is not established, it would incur the fault of lacking a homologous example (*sapakṣa*).

Indeed, there is no such fault of [the argument] being established [by default], because these things are likewise considered sentient beings; for instance, like that which is not said to be "separated from appropriation" (*anupātta*) because it is not an appropriated thing (*upāttavastu*), yet this too is not an appropriated thing, just as tiles and wood, or an anthill, because they do not belong to the category of sentient beings.
For what reason is it not admitted that the hell-wardens, dogs, crows, and so forth, belong to the category of sentient beings?
For they are likewise seen to possess the form, the physical power, and the capacity for movement of sentient beings, and they do not depend upon external causal conditions, just like other beings.
If that were so, it would follow that all causes are unestablished.
This objection is irrational, for all the movements of those in the hells do not depend upon external conditions.
Because those hell-beings are moved by the sustaining power of their prior sinful karma, they appear like the dancing shadows of wood, resembling sentient beings.
Furthermore, since that state is certainly not a sentient being—as it is not included among the five destinies—it is like wood or stone.
From this it is known that they certainly cannot be of the same class as the other beings born in evil states.
For while other beings born in evil states who are born in this place likewise undergo all the common sufferings found here, those [beings] do not undergo these sufferings.

Because the sentient beings in those realms do not experience the same shared suffering as one another—just as the Garland-Bearers (*mālādhāra*) and others are not denizens of hell (*nāraka*)—yet all those born in the evil states experience this suffering together, due to their common karma arising simultaneously in this place.
If it were otherwise, even birth [in such a place] would be difficult to obtain, let alone being subjected to harm.

Although this logic holds, the fact that the hell-wardens and others do not experience that suffering does not constitute a joint accomplishment; this is not the correct explanation, because they are born there without experiencing the same suffering of harm.
Because those who do not inflict harm are nonetheless like those who harm living beings, they are equally scorched and experience suffering together.
If one were to further argue that the path consists of mutual harming and vexation, then it would follow that those born there must experience suffering at times.

This too is unreasonable, because at the time they are mutually harming one another, the distinction between "this one is a hell-being" and "this one is a *pāra* [guard]" would be lost from their ranks.
Because they are capable of inflicting harm and possess functional activity, they are described as wardens by virtue of being the conditions [for suffering].

If this is the case for one, it should be so for the others as well; thus, both would possess the nature of a warden, which is inseparable from the very essence of the hell-beings themselves, thereby resulting in a logical contradiction.
Because they do not possess the nature of hell-wardens, they are like the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa heaven.

This is intended to clarify that those in the *nāraka* (hell) realm are not victims of harm; for if it were admitted that they inflict harm upon one another, then the logic would require that they treat each other with equal reciprocity. Knowing their own strength, physical stature, and so forth, and thus mutually deceiving one another, they ought not to give rise to fear.
Even if one were to see that [being] of immense stature and, upon measuring one's own prowess, conceive the thought of superiority—once this is known, how could fear possibly remain?
How could it be like the denizens of hell seeing the wardens and their ilk?
How much more so when their physical dimensions and vital strength are no different, yet upon seeing them, one gives rise to thoughts of fear?

Furthermore, since both are jailers, their physical dimensions are identical and their bodily strength is equal; there being no difference in strength between them, it stands to reason that they must possess distinct physical dimensions and unequal degrees of courage and ferocity, such that upon seeing them, fear is produced.

When calculating time in this manner, as those of the hell-realm are undergoing their suffering, they see the wardens approaching and give rise to great terror; the fire of grief erupts from within, completely burning their chests, and as continuous suffering arises, their bodies tremble and quiver.
Beings born of evil karma undergo such afflictions that even those of skillful means and clear wisdom are unable to fully comprehend the matter.

This stage of existence is inherently contradictory; yet it is observed in the world that there are those who harbor malicious intentions and a heart like aconite poison, desiring to harm others and instill in them fear and dread.
Although they are situated in places that are extremely heavy, dreadful, and terrifying, and though they are restrained there, these beings do not give rise to fear like those who are cowardly.

Nevertheless, because such beings possess hearts of hardness and are frequently seen [in such states], those in the hells who suffer from torment often harbor such terror that their bodies seem as if they were melting away; therefore, the denizens of hell are not the ones who inflict harm.
It is like an animal tied to a pillar at a slaughterhouse; for while this [pillar] is the cause of its fear, it does not experience the suffering [inflicted by the butcher].
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ratnasambhava-śāstra*, Fascicle Two.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ratnasambhava-śāstra*, Fascicle Three. Also known as the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratā-sūtra-anuvyākhyāna-śāstra*.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by imperial decree.
The treatise states:
The Narakapāla hell is like a hunter of deer; this should be understood in such a way.

Not only do they not undergo the suffering of mutual harm, but they also do not experience the collective suffering of the vessel-world (bhājana-loka), for these hell-wardens are capable of inflicting harm upon them.

If it were otherwise, when they are undergoing the suffering of being scorched upon ground of molten, boiling red-hot iron and are unable to endure it, how could they at that time oppress and harm others?

When their bodies move and shift upon this scorching ground, even the limbs and joints of these hell-beings can no longer support themselves; how much less could they possibly perform any other action?

However, they can only float and boil amidst molten iron; their bodies are controlled by others and they possess not even a fraction of autonomy. Yet those hell-wardens are valiant and capable of harming others; therefore, it is certain that they do not experience that suffering themselves, just as a cook stands at a distance holding an iron shovel to turn the frying fish within hot oil.

Alternatively, if one were to take the hell-wardens (*yamadūta*) as being among the denizens of hell (*nāraka*), this would contradict the definition of a warder, because they lack the capacity to inflict mutual harm upon one another.

Furthermore, when the various classes of denizens of hell are undergoing burning and torment, they are unable to harm each other; if that were the case, they would not be warders at all. Thus, for one who establishes the thesis that "denizens of hell" (*nāraka*) and "hell-wardens" (*naraka-pāla*) [are distinct], there is the fault of contradicting their own position.

Furthermore, if it is argued that because they experience the touch of that intensely painful hot iron, the denizens of hell cannot harm them—just as one might place a living creature amidst glowing coals—then [the following applies].

Alternatively, it may be that those of this class do not experience such suffering, as is the case with the Tuṣita Heaven; this demonstrates that the hell-wardens (*yamarāja*) are not themselves *nāraka* beings.

Thus, regarding this point, the outsider’s alternative interpretation—which cites scriptural authority as proof—is utterly erroneous. Nevertheless, for the sake of those with limited intelligence, I have briefly set forth these outlines to expose their biased views.
He then raised an objection, saying:
"I do not accept that there are those among the class of hell-wardens in the hells who do not experience suffering,
as it is stated in the Sūtra:"
"O Bhikṣus! There is a hell named Ṣaṭsparśāyatana. If sentient beings are born therein, whenever they look at various forms with their eyes, they see only things that are utterly unattractive."
In truth, those sentient beings do possess such qualities; yet since the hell-wardens are not sentient beings, what could they possibly perceive?
To insist on this while refusing to admit that they are sentient beings is nothing more than a gathering together to chew upon empty space.
He raises an objection, saying:

"When those in the various hells undergo their sufferings, there are distinctions among them because they obtain different bodies, as in the case of one who has committed a single *ānantarya* sin versus one who has committed many *ānantarya* sins."
This also fails to account for the intended meaning, as previously stated.

When sentient beings born in the *naraka* hells experience acute suffering, while excluding the specific poisons of suffering belonging to other realms, they nevertheless undergo all the common sufferings present within those hells.
However, in those places, due to the fierce gales of the winds of heavy karma, one undergoes extreme suffering; yet this is not experienced by those who have committed no uninterrupted [sin].
Because it is not experienced in the same way as those various types of uninterrupted and violent sufferings, it is therefore considered indeterminate.

To clarify this matter, apart from those hell-wardens (*yamarāja*), there is no such distinction among the other denizens of hell (*nāraka*), for they all experience the same suffering common to that realm.
Thus, since the established thesis has no locus where it would differ from another thesis, how could the principle of its arising be considered indeterminate?
However, because they experience suffering simultaneously with those in the uninterrupted hells (*avīci*),
an external objection is raised:
"The claim that the hell-wardens (*yamadūta*) do not experience suffering is not a valid answer, as it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)."
However, one should not make such a definitive judgment, seeing that because one being suffers, others must likewise do so.
We clearly observe this phenomenon in the world: for instance, when a sheep or a camel is stung by a scorpion, it dies immediately, and a portion of its flesh is taken as food by birds.
Furthermore, based on the fact that such differences exist among animals, we likewise observe within the human realm those who do not experience suffering, such as the man afflicted with a tumor.

A physician would then step upon a heated iron plate and immediately press his hot foot against the site of the ailment; although the patient undergoes extreme agony, the physician’s foot never experiences pain. Nevertheless, sentient beings are in reality no different from one another.
This is also because the suffering that arises simultaneously with the *naraka* realm is not perceived; therefore, it is not designated as "naraka.

To claim that seeing things such as venomous stings can sever the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is merely a display of extensive learning and clever worldly knowledge; it has no bearing on the matters discussed here that accord with the ultimate truth.

If it is argued that, according to this school, one is included within a particular realm of rebirth simply by virtue of similarity to that realm, and that because one observes within such a realm beings who do not experience the suffering characteristic of that realm, the opposing school's position suffers from the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*), this too fails to understand my established meaning: namely, that there is a definitive suffering inherent to whatever realm of rebirth one has attained.
Because that which is not shared is established as the primary function of the preceding [karma], yet humans or animals are not born in those destinies (*gati*).

According to that principle, one must necessarily experience [the result] and yet does not; for instance, when sheep and the like encounter the venom of a scorpion, they suffer the pain of death, or they experience the agony produced by hot feet. If these were entirely not experienced, then because they would be the suffering of those destinies, it would follow that the nature of those destinies could not exist—such would be the fault.
There is another interpretation which states:

"However, the hell-guardians are produced through the predominant influence of the karma of themselves and others; because they are not harmed [by the punishments], they inflict suffering upon one another. This is not accepted by others.
I now say to you: being attached to your own views with a deluded mind, even if you were in empty space, you would stumble at every step.
Since one does not suffer harm from another in the Nāraka-parāyaṇa [hell], all the suffering produced by the oppression of others will certainly not be experienced; this is what is asserted.
However, if one maintains that [the bound] does not experience the suffering of bodily injury from that [agent], with whom would it cooperate?
To this, the following rebuttal is made:
although there is indeed this mutual harming, the distinction between states is caused by the difference in their functions, just as there is a distinction between the bound and the binder.

In that case, you would be using your own words to refute your own tenet, for it is impossible for that which is not simultaneous to function as the binder and the bound in a relationship of mutual fettering.
If you claim that those two exist sequentially, this too is irrational; for one is not called "bound" merely by undergoing bondage, nor does one become a "binder" merely by binding another.
However, even if these two were to follow one another in the sequence of suffering, they could not be established as existing within the hells (*naraka*).

If it were not the hell realm when one experiences agonizing and extreme pain, yet it were the hell realm when one is harmed by others or encounters their afflictions, then one could not admit that a single continuum possesses both birth and death; for this would constitute a great logical error.
Since they harm one another at the same time and cannot coexist, it is not a single moment [of consciousness] that is the perpetrator; thus, it cannot be the agent of this plan.

If one attempts to offer a rebuttal by shifting the argument, claiming that although they belong to the same realm (*gati*), their names differ due to differences in function—one being called a *nāraka* (hell-being) and the other a hell-guardian—just as within the human realm there are those who are not prison guards yet are still bound in shackles.
This is also unreasonable, because [the hells] do not depend upon them.

Since the denizens of hell (*naraka*) are said to be like those who are bound by virtue of not relying on or depending upon specific functional differences, yet this [bondage] occurs solely due to the realm of existence (*gati*) acting as the cause, how then could they abandon their wardens?

Therefore, it is certain that there are distinctions among the stages (*avasthā*). This is because the objects of transition (*gati*) do not act as the causal conditions for one another; furthermore, the distinction between the bound (*baddha*) and the binder (*bandhana*) arises from the difference in their functions. Consequently, it is logically appropriate to establish distinct stages in accordance with those differences, and there is certainly no contradiction in this.
If it is granted that there are distinct levels within the state of pleasure, then one must likewise grant that the *nārakas* (denizens of hell) are not themselves the hell-wardens (*yamarākṣasa*).
This alone is the essential point of my own school, for it accords perfectly with the previously established proof.
If it is admitted that the nature of hell-beings exists substantially, then because their functions differ, they may at times be designated as "hell-wardens";
thus, the various stages of this view would be established without fault. However, this would entail the admission of distinct classes and divergent paths.
As a verse says:
"One who is full of anger commits cruel deeds; One who delights in performing sinful acts And rejoices at seeing the suffering of others Shall be reborn as a henchman of Yama."
Since hell-beings do not possess these characteristics,
if this *gaṇa* were of definitive meaning, how could one suddenly speak in such a manner as to say that its wardens and others do not belong to the category of sentient beings?
What contradiction is there in reasoning if one speaks in this way according to the appearances perceived by those in hell?
Those with limited vision, because they take the specific movements and behaviors of others as their objects of cognition, infer the state of those minds.

However, when the seeds within consciousness originally ripen, conceptualization arises according to the specific distinctions of their respective appearances. It was in accordance with what those beings perceived that the Buddha made this statement, desiring to cause sentient beings with evil karma to sever their sinful views by manifesting the retribution of suffering born of evil karma in the most horrific places of the *naraka* hells.
According to their respective perspectives and views, they speak of disagreeable things as existing outside of consciousness;
yet, when discussing the actual reality with certainty, all are merely internal conditions appearing as semblances, and thus there is certainly no contradiction.
There is another interpretation which states:

Although they mutually inflict suffering and harm upon one another, these hierarchical distinctions do not deviate from the general rule; for at this time, there is no fixed status, such that those who are harmed are called *nāraka* (denizens of hell) and those who inflict harm are termed *pāla* (wardens).
Therefore, it is certain that when those in the various hells (*nāraka*) are actually being harmed, there is no possibility of the fault of [the hell-beings] themselves becoming the wardens.
When one adheres to this position, does it ever produce even a fraction of a reason for us to find pleasure in the functional utility of the wardens as we have established them?
Some say that these various manifestations arise from the power of karma; as they follow sentient beings, they do not remain uniform.

Because they previously tormented and harmed one another, they now undergo execution and slaughter together in the hells, mutually oppressing and harming each other while enduring all manner of suffering.
If there are living beings who, lacking the physical strength to harm others themselves, know only how to endure suffering and have no leisure for anything else,
it is because those sentient beings were previously mutual enemies that they now inflict suffering and harm upon one another.

All those who are hell-beings (*nāraka*) here engage in mutual harm with one another; this is not permitted by any external agent, for it arises from the manifestation of consciousness according to their own respective karma.
To claim that because they do not possess the nature of a hell-guardian (*yamadūta*), they are incapable of inflicting harm, is an erroneous statement entirely devoid of logical sense.

If it is granted that the victim is a denizen of hell (*nāraka*), yet the inflictor does not undergo such suffering, some say that among those of the same realm (*gati*), it is not necessarily required that the various types of hell-guards be identical in physical form or dimensions; nevertheless, their appearance is cruel, poisonous, and terrifying, inspiring fear upon being seen, with massive bodies of extraordinary and formidable strength.

Even if there were a physical form and size that could be accommodated as being similar, their bodies are nonetheless poisonous and terrifying; like those of the Mlecchas, one is struck with dread upon seeing them, for they are capable of inflicting harm.

Even if such a person’s physical stature is short and stunted, because their innate nature is fierce and sharp, they treat even an opponent of great physical form as insignificant as a blade of grass; they despise and belittle that host with ample strength, yet they still have not mastered the profound and subtle meanings of others' intentions.
Nevertheless, I shall forgive that oversight for now.
The matter of the various hell-beings (*nāraka*) harming one another is no different; their physical forms, powers, and sizes must necessarily be similar.
Although such a statement may occasionally be made, one might immediately raise an objection based on the momentum of that argument, saying:
"It is not necessarily required that their forms and dimensions be similar.
With whom, then, do you intend to engage in this debate?
Those who estimate their own prowess and strength, and thus feel no fear when facing others in a decisive contest—
such a claim is truly a meaningless statement, for it arises from either cruelty or mere intimidation.
Because one gives rise to extreme terror due to being completely oppressed, it is not the case that the harmer establishes this path when it is being accomplished;

to do so would constitute a logical fallacy. To clarify these distinct characteristics through skillful means, you now further establish both cruelty and majesty; this, however, becomes a great act of kindness, serving as a virtuous companion that increases my own radiance.

As stated above, having attained distinct bodies, they experience different hells and various sufferings; yet, due to the power of their karma, some may not even feel the pain of being burned by fierce fires.
Were it not for a virtuous friend, who else could have ventured to speak such words?

For one who is a close friend and naturally good, they always provide benefit and kindness regardless of whether circumstances are favorable or perilous; it was with the desire to demonstrate that [the Buddha] would not suffer the pain of burning that he made this statement.

However, at this point, assisting in the establishment of the argument serves to reveal the intention of the virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*); because he does not accept that suffering, he intends to establish that [the subject] is not a hell-being (*nāraka*).
Now it is further stated:
"It is due to the power of karma that one speaks of a great fire.
To say that [the fire] does not burn is precisely what establishes the meaning of Vijñaptimātra (Cognition-Only).

Since there is no real fire, and it is solely the power of karma that can destroy its own nature, and since one has already determined that such suffering is not experienced, it follows that this fire’s own nature is fundamentally non-existent.

However, the existence of a real nature is what is accepted by our own school. If one were to accept that the entity of the manifest appearance of consciousness is fundamentally non-existent—claiming that there is no real fire because of the power of karma—this would be logically consistent, as it is delimited by the force of prior karma.
If it were otherwise, since the fruit summoned by that predominant karma is already present, why would it not be seen?
It would be like an ignorant person who, wishing to extinguish a fire, pours more clarified butter upon it.
This causes the Vijñānavāda school to flourish even more brilliantly.
By these various principles,
it is proven that this [consciousness] does not constitute the category of hell-beings (nāraka).
If it were not established as a type of hell-being (*naraka*), what logical harm would there be in its being a hungry ghost (*preta*) or an animal (*tiryagyoni*)?
If that were so, since it is not a hell-being, how could it be born in an evil destination (*durgati*)?
Because one does not attain another realm of existence, one is born in *naraka*.
If that were so, once born there, one would be identical to those in *naraka*.
Furthermore, how could it be admitted that the process of birth exists in that place?

If one is born there, one should belong to that same homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*); yet at the very moment of initial birth, it could not possibly exist, because being categorized as a sentient being (*sattva-saṃkhyāta*) is not admitted [at that stage].
Furthermore, this is because there is no uncertainty regarding the sentient beings belonging to that same realm of rebirth (*gati*).

If one maintains that this view is what constitutes "birth," then even those of great majestic power are found here in the realm of *naraka* (hell) for the sake of saving sentient beings from the suffering they ought to relieve; since these individuals, though not of the class of hell-beings, are nonetheless seen to exist there, the argument becomes inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

This statement is not made based on the observation that this [realm] is always and invariably perceived as such; rather, the intention here is to argue that it is seen to exist only within the evil destinies, specifically in the *naraka* hells. At that time, when the various Yama kings and their retinues of messengers go forth, they must necessarily follow him; at that moment, those kings along with their attendants do not exit the boundaries [of the hell].
If that realm were of no distinct categories, how could there also be animals among the gods?
For instance, celestial elephants and the like, though not belonging to the divine destiny (*devagati*), are nonetheless born there.
In this way, the various classes of hell-wardens in the realm of King Yama, as well as dogs, crows, and the like—even those who do not belong to that class—are born therein.
By this principle, they are identical to the *nāraka*s (denizens of hell); when the hell-wardens and others are born in hell, they are subsumed within that very destiny (*gati*).
Why is this? Because they arise in the same location.
It is precisely by this principle that it can be established as certain: one must undergo that suffering.
This defense is not tenable; although one may be born in hell, one is not a *nāraka*.
Why? Because the experience [of suffering] is not the same.

Regarding the fact that animals exist in the heavens whereas they do not in the hells: there is no distinction among the various realms of animals and gods; just as in the hells (*naraka*) and other such places, their respective karmas produce different results, so too those beings experience suffering in accordance with the power of their own karma.

Therefore, it is certain that among animals in the heavenly realms there must be those who possess karma capable of inducing heavenly bliss; only then would they be born in heaven to experience that same pleasure together, for they are produced by karma conducive to happiness.

Regarding the claim that animals and hungry ghosts do not experience those sufferings: all those born among the animal and hungry ghost realms undergo various kinds of suffering within their respective rebirth states.
It is not so; why then do the various hell-wardens and others not experience that suffering?

From this, it is known that the suffering of *naraka* (hell) is not a retribution for birth (*upapadyavedanīya*), because it is experienced as part of the course of action (*karmagati*), just as in the case of Nalada and others.
If that were so, since one would be born there even without karma, this has already been analyzed at length above.
That which appears therein as being induced by the power of karma is not a valid analogy; thus, what they have established is definitely unproven and is not accepted by us.
However, within this [hell], because things such as iron mountains momentarily separate and momentarily join, there is purposeful activity.
Other masters say that those hell-wardens and others also experience that suffering.

That being so, since the reasons and analogies you have stated are inconsistent and contradict one another, you ought to further explain that they are based on different foundations; or perhaps, due to the distinct power of karma over the increasing fire, one does not experience suffering.
Why is this? Because if one does not accept [this], that statement would be flawed.
Others further say:

It is as if there were locations for feeling within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) despite the absence of painful or pleasant feelings; yet, because those who feel possess that which is felt, this [objection] is likewise [invalid].

Such a view is irrational, for since sentient beings born in the formless realm do not possess a physical vessel [of a body], there are no locations, feelings, or formations (*saṃskāra*) in that realm.
How, then, are they apprehended by spatial dimensions?
Because spatial dimensions serve as causes—that is, because that which possesses spatial dimensions serves as a cause—it should be understood in this way:
in reality there are no spatial dimensions; there is only arising.
Sentient beings born in the two realms of desire and form have accumulated causes; therefore, their birth must possess spatial dimensions.
Just as the realm of form possesses spatial dimensions, so too does the realm of desire, because it is the cause of that [higher] realm.
This is not so; because they are formless and lack a place of residence, it would be unreasonable [to claim otherwise], just as in the case of those who are not conjoined.

If that were the case, one must admit that those *nāraka* beings arise through the predominant power of karma, producing distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*), for they are not comprised within the category of sentient beings (*sattva*).

The primary elements, such as earth, arise within the hells with distinct differences in shape, color, and magnitude; just as there are variations in the appearance and so forth of sentient beings, as well as differences in the size and strength of their hands, feet, and limbs, as well as their height, length, and bulk—it is through these functions therein that they are designated as "executioners" and the like.
If that is so, how is it that non-sentient things, such as thunderbolts and the like, perform various functions of hands, feet, and body parts without depending on external conditions?
It is because [the Buddha] desires to instill great terror in them that he manifests various superior powers, moving his hands, feet, and so forth.
This is due to the wind element causing the hands and feet to move, manifesting various distinct actions; the power of that wind acts according to the person's intentions and thoughts.
It is the same for all those in the hells; as soon as they see this, they give rise to fear.
Those beings in the hells experience great terror due to the power of their karma.

It is just as a wooden man who can perform various actions; through the combination of the great elements, although he lacks thought or consciousness, by the power of karma and conditions, such appearances as the movement of hands and feet are manifested as distinct activities.

The principle that insentient things can be established as such is accepted; for in those locations, through the sovereign power of the karma of hell-beings, they themselves perceive mountains of rams and the like appearing and disappearing.

This is not a sentient being, yet it is nonetheless perceived; thus, the distinctions such as the dwelling places and the ground, as well as the fact that the hell-wardens and others are not sentient beings, are logically established, and there is no need for further confusion.
This is not that there is no object of perception; rather, it is because the mental dispositions (*āśaya*) of the hell-wardens and others give rise [to such perceptions].

Those wardens, as well as the ground and other locations, are represented by different shapes and forms to indicate the hells and so forth. It is accepted that through the power of karma, the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) such as earth arise within the hells as specific transformations of shape and form, including the movement of hands and feet and the various locations and primary elements. Alternatively, some of these bonds and so forth may be absent due to the power of karma.
This principle should not be untenable.
For what reason is it not accepted?

Consciousness undergoes such a transformation through the power of karma, just as the combination of forms and so forth seen in a dream gives rise to external reflections that manifest various appearances; thus, the functional activity of transformation should be universally acknowledged.
Consciousness undergoes such a transformation through the power of karma that it appears contrary to its actual location.
If one grants that this occurs through the power of karma, what need is there for distinct primary elements (*mahābhūta*)?

This is because the various hell-wardens and others are merely specific transformations and movements—such as the raising and lowering of hands and feet—of the four primary elements; because they are like forms and locations seen in a dream; because their shapes lack substantiality or function; or because they do not possess the distinct characteristics of earth and the other elements, as was previously stated regarding the mountain of rams and so forth.
Because he does not allow for the transformation of material form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), the same applies to emanations (*nirmāṇa*); differences in shape and so forth arise through the power of another.

These arise from the transformation of consciousness (*vijñāna-pariṇāma*); various distinct appearances manifest as differing forms and postures, and apart from consciousness, there is not a single thing that exists which can be perceived.
Regarding this, an external objection is raised:

If it is merely through the transformation of consciousness that various distinct forms and appearances—such as the perception of hell-guardians—are produced from one's own consciousness, then since they share the same cause of suffering, the *nārakas* (denizens of hell) would not be [distinct from] the hell-guardians. [This is because] these four great elements (*mahābhūta*) arise from the same karma as a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*). Furthermore, at the time of experiencing suffering, [the guardians and the denizens] do not experience it in the same way; therefore, it is necessary to speak of the four great elements.
What has been stated thus does not effectively refute the opposing school. Why is it ineffective?
Because it merely asserts that sentient beings perceive the transformations of their own consciousness as hell-wardens and the like, who are then able to inflict cruelty and poison.
Due to the manifestation within their own respective consciousnesses, each person perceives the executioners and various instruments of harm; thus, they do not contradict one another.

However, just as these perceptions of suffering and harm appear as similar reflections because their causes are identical, the experience of suffering is simultaneous. Whether the activities performed by the teacher and the disciple are the same or different, one forcibly asserts that they are the same regarding those differing actions.

Furthermore, because solitary hells (pratyeka-naraka) do not see one another and their sufferings are not shared, the principle of the primary elements (mahābhūta) being established there is logically untenable.
As for the "karmic perfuming in other locations," this refers to those who maintain that hell-beings (nāraka) arise through the specific causal power of their own karma.
It is logically necessary to admit that the perfuming of those karmas resides within the continuum of consciousness, because by the power of karma, they do not accumulate elsewhere.

When karma acts upon the earth and other elements, it unites cause and effect; thus, this very place serves as the locus for the fruition of that habituation. Therein, various types of forms are produced according to their respective distinctions through the conjunction of conditions, such as the consciousnesses of images like walls and so forth, which arise from specific combinations of causes. These various categories of form should be distinguished accordingly.

It is not so; because these primary elements (*mahābhūta*) are combined and accumulated through the power of karma as their cause, the fruit is produced through the differentiation of the continuity of that karma.

One should understand it thus: because one’s own continuity attains the fruit of meditative concentration, the cultivation and recollection take the seed as their object; furthermore, there is no distinction between the continuities of different sentient beings.

Having understood this, the reason for taking up a small portion, such as a single individual, is to demonstrate that the internal perfuming of the mind and mental factors within the continuum—which constitutes the distinct results subsumed under the five destinies—is produced by the habitual tendencies of one's own karma.

Just as the fruit of the latencies of the formless realm is not a separate non-associated formation apart from the mind and mental factors, so too here it is merely a difference in terminology regarding the entity;
there is no difference in substance. Therefore, this is spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*).

Alternatively, because the entities of the mind and mental factors are not separate, yet their natures differ and their bases of arising are distinct, for those who have not yet abandoned desire, the perfuming of form arises according to its own power in its respective base of arising, because its activity is established therein.

Just as with the karma that perfumes the formless realm, or because the mind and mental factors are not produced apart from the primary elements (mahābhūta) of the form-sphere, it is only through the conjunction of karmic forces that they can arise.
Alternatively, because the continuity of consciousness abides as the fruit of perfuming (*vāsanā*), it is likewise with [states] such as memory, affection, and aversion.

The transformation of consciousness into the images of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is also not separate from consciousness; yet, regarding the distinctions in their shapes and forms, it is asserted that the fruit exists elsewhere.
Regarding the statement that "the perfumed consciousness possesses a fruit": this is because it serves as the cause for the fruit of what has been cultivated.
Other masters say: "It is solely through the power of its own substance that it transforms into a fruit."
Birth in the desire and form realms occurs because consciousness is perfumed by the power of karma and serves as its basis.
Just as in the formless realm, birth occurs through the accumulation and perfuming of karma.
That which is described as the perfuming based upon indeterminate consciousness, along with the associated fruits of the remaining collection of consciousnesses, should not exist [in those realms].
Therefore, it is said that the basis [of the self] encompasses all sentient beings, or else it should be attained without effort.
Furthermore, there is another explanation:
the karmic fruits of one's own actions exist within a single body as cause and effect; thus, they are established in the same manner as the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Since karma is the cause of differentiation, it would follow that there could be no distinct arrangement of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the body as a result;

if that were the case, then for other persons, the basis (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*)—namely, the body and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—would likewise lack differentiation in their shared activity. Furthermore, because they are designated as sentient beings, they would constitute a single stream of continuity together with the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
In that case, it is not that the sentient beings of hell are established through a combination of the great elements (mahābhūta) based on a sudden differentiation of perceptions;

therefore, there is a distinction in their continuity. Furthermore, when a consciousness in a continuous stream, acting as a dominant cause, gives rise to various distinct types of separate consciousnesses, at that time there must be the successive arising of causes and effects with distinct continuities.
It is not so; why? This is precisely because one intends to explain the distinction of causes.

For example, the seeds within the continuity and conjunction of the mind are the establishing cause (*pratiṣṭhā-hetu*); what is stated here refers only to the cause that establishes [the support], and does not state that consciousness is the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) as the basis.

From this seed, there arises a differentiation of consciousness through uninterrupted succession; however, it is only by means of the continuity of the seed's own essence that transformation and birth occur.
As for what is called "predominant," just as the earth and other elements can only act as conditions, so too should the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute them be understood.
This is also not the case; when [the elements] arise from their own seeds, they are said to have these [seeds] as their sole condition.

Otherwise, there would be separate seeds of the four great elements arising from the continuum of consciousness, just as when one dies in the formless realm and is born in the realm of form, those dominant fruits (adhipatiphala) are obtained through the maturation of karma (*vipāka-karma*) and function as the requisites for enjoyment, just like the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
This is produced by the continuity of one's own karma, which is desirable and pleasant; this correct principle accords with the results of consciousness as transformed, as taught in the Āgamas.

As for the reason why some do not accept it: it is because they forcibly construct and fabricate [their views] through irrational and deviant attachments based on their own perspectives. Who could possibly claim that the result of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) contradicts the Āgamas?
For what reason do so many Āgama sūtras not establish *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only)?
Since there are no forms and other objects apart from consciousness-only, one should not separately speak of the existence of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

Nevertheless, one should understand that wholesome and other such phenomena are established without departing from those consciousnesses and the twelve bases; thus, there must be bases such as form, because this was taught by the Buddha.
If [the object] were excluded from form and so forth, its establishment would be untenable, as it would contradict the Buddha’s words.
Alternatively, because the substance of form and so forth exists substantially, just like the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*), for this was spoken by the Buddha.
Consciousness and form, etc., are likewise not distinct entities, just as in the case of the *dharmāyatana*.
This reasoning is untenable; what is stated here does not negate *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Why is this so?
Based on those beings born by transformation, the Blessed One, with a specific underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*), taught that there are sense-bases such as form.

Just as with "beings born by transformation"—when the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke of the existence of beings born by transformation, his underlying intention was merely that the continuum of the mind proceeds unbroken to future lives; he did not mean that beings born by transformation exist substantially.

The underlying intention of this statement is as follows: in order to discipline a certain class of sentient beings, the Buddha said that there are sentient beings born by transformation; this was spoken with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

This refers to those sentient beings who are harmed by the view of nihilism—those who act according to their own whims, who deny the existence of future lives, and who deny the causality of good and evil—and it is for the purpose of washing away such evil views that it is said that the continuum of the mind is uninterrupted.

The term "continuity of mind" (citta-saṃtati) indicates that [the being] is to be born; because the principle applies equally to dying here and being born there, it is said that there is "apparitional birth" (upapāduka) when the continuity is uninterrupted—this is the underlying intention (saṃdhi).
Apart from consciousness, there is no separate self; how is this known to be so?
As it is said in the sūtra:
"There is no self and no sentient beings, but only dharmas because of causes."
The sūtra is not like that; for that sūtra does not state that sentient beings both exist and do not exist.
Therefore, because it does not contradict the sūtra, the expression "continuum of mind" indicates that it is uninterrupted and capable of proceeding to future lives.
In this way, it should be understood that, just as with the sense bases such as form, this was spoken with a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya*) for the sake of maturing a certain class of sentient beings.
Therefore, there is no fault of contradicting one's own teaching (*svaśāsana-virodha*) in what has been established.
The reason established in this manner is also not definitive. Why is this?

According to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the Buddha taught that there are separately existing beings born by transformation (*upapāduka-sattva*); however, he never said that apart from the aggregates of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), there exist separately any wholesome or unwholesome states, nor their fruits, or any other sentient beings.

Because this reason is inconclusive, the Buddha taught that for those who hold the view of annihilationism and deny future lives, the continuum of the mind of a Tathāgata remains uninterrupted; he provisionally designates a "sentient being" within that aggregate of consciousness, and thus spoke of its existence within a concise formulation.
There are four intentions regarding the absence of objects apart from the mind.
What are these four? First, the intentional meaning; second, the objective sphere; third, the manifestation of the result; and fourth, the meaning of the intentional terminology.

Bound by conceptual discrimination, these causal conditions are explained as the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*); all of these should be established, and questions and answers should be raised in their proper sequence according to reason.
What is the underlying intention (*saṃdhāya*) behind the teaching of the twelve bases (*āyatana*)?
There are sentient beings who, like the continuity of the mind, possess an uninterrupted succession.
It is said that sentient beings are able to establish the signifier and the signified within the mind, grasping at them as having the form of objective entities.
In this context, the objects of the spheres of form and so forth, as well as sound, should be distinguished in this way:

consciousness arises from its own seeds and manifests with an appearance resembling the object, thereby functioning as the internal and external bases (*āyatana*). The Buddha taught that these are ten because, from those [internal] bases such as the eye, there arise those [external] bases such as form.
It should be understood according to reason that in those two places, these characteristics of seeds and that consciousness are explained.
As the Blessed One said:

"In order to establish the sense bases and so forth, he spoke of commonly accepted distinctions such as 'the eye' and so on; this was intended to establish that blue and other objects appear with clear manifestation."

Those similar forms arise from that consciousness; because the seeds of that consciousness have been established as particularly superior in those who have not yet abandoned desire, those very seeds are able to produce them.

Although it is provisionally established, the fruit has not yet been experienced; until one attains the power of corresponding conditions, within the continuous succession of moment-to-moment arising and ceasing, one acquires a subtle nature that undergoes skillful differentiation and transformation to attain excellence. This is like rice, wheat, and so forth, which, through the convergence of conditions such as the earth, grow and increase; their natures differ as they successively establish themselves, resulting in the appearance of sprouts and other stages.
Just as it is with external seeds of such a nature, so it is internally.

This internal mental continuum manifests in the present; in the interval of a single uninterrupted moment, it is capable of producing the distinct natures of blue and other colors. Yet these seeds are called the "eye-element" (*cakṣur-dhātu*); as they successively manifest as their respective resultant natures, the mind and mental factors establish this form as its "eye-base" (*cakṣur-āyatana*).

It is also like this: when such distinctions of form manifest, the essence of consciousness, in conjunction with the seeds of blue and so forth within the *ālayavijñāna*, awakens them. Due to the non-manifest consciousness, it is able to awaken the distinctions in the self-nature of the transformation of images, just as when objects such as crystal, lapis lazuli, or mica are wrapped in thin materials, a consciousness arises that manifests according to the colors of those underlying substances. This is what the Blessed One, through reasoned analysis, has taught as the sense-field of form (*rūpāyatana*).

However, within our own school’s teachings, it is said that because the consciousnesses of those [objects] differ in form, abide differently, and provide different benefits, this matter is designated as the "form base" (*rūpāyatana*). In this way, up to the images of consciousness such as solidity, moisture, warmth, and so forth, the power and function of their respective bases and objects are most predominant; these are the phenomena produced by the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

Since the seeds, their characteristics, and their manifestations arise as the objects of perception through the various transformations of sounds, names, and so forth, the ālayavijñāna must likewise be established as that which possesses the distinct functional capacities for the segmentation of form.

Those who possess wisdom discern and analyze each part individually, explaining the distinctions in the arrangement of the internal and external bases (*āyatana*); this is the underlying intent (*saṃdhi*).

Just as the elements (*dhātu*) are established, so too is the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) established, which arises in dependence upon the element of mind (*manas-dhātu*) and the six [bases].
Thus, although the nature of the mental element (*manodhātu*) differs [from the others], it is nonetheless said that there are eighteen elements (*dhātus*).

Just as the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) serves as the seed for the eye-consciousness and so forth in succession, it is designated as the "eye-base" (*cakṣurāyatana*) and so on when it manifests distinctly.
Why is it called a "seed"?

It is because it is able to produce various entities such as sprouts and so forth, possessing distinct natures. This is like the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), which are universally accepted as producing sprouts and other things of their own kind; thus, it is called a seed because it produces specific distinctions.

It is just as with seeds such as rice and wheat, which are commonly acknowledged in the world to possess distinct natures that are not of a single kind, yet are capable of producing the eye and visual consciousness, along with their correspondence to a second moment; from these two realms, there arises that nature of alertness established in accordance with those conditions. It does not arise as a single entity at a single time, because—just as with a single mental factor—it is able to produce immeasurable varieties of form-nature individually.

This is also the case here: the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) is either identical to or distinct from the sense bases such as the eye, because its own substance is distinct at the moment the consciousness arises; thus, the ripening consciousness constitutes the sense bases such as the eye.
That form is subtle, and because the various functions of the consciousnesses arising from the eye and other sense faculties differ, it is extremely difficult to perceive.
Furthermore, it is not as if there were separate eyes and so forth, or that [the consciousness] would take the purified four great elements as its object, such as visible form.

Furthermore, according to a specific Āgama, the Buddha stated that the visible and resistant matter derived from the four great elements—such as the fleshly eye and so forth—is pure; this applies likewise, up to and including the body and other such faculties.
This image of improper cognition is spoken of with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*).

Therefore, the four great elements are not separate from the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of consciousness; nor do they take the cognition of blue and so forth as their seeds, because such cognitions involve attachment to signs (*nimitta*).
