Even in states such as dreaming, there is the direct perception of various objects such as forms, just as has been stated.
Regarding the statement "because the mind that conceals and examines exists," this reveals that the reason established here suffers from the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Nevertheless, due to being impaired by dreams, cataracts, or a mind characterized by transgressions, things appear as if clearly perceived before distinct sense faculties.
Although there is no real external object, there is the occurrence of seeing; furthermore, this does not transcend the essential nature of consciousness.
It is for the purpose of discernment that one presently receives and accepts the objects being experienced.

By this reasoning, if one intends to establish that real objects such as form exist independently of consciousness, there is the fault of contradiction; it is merely a matter of arrogant pride, and furthermore, there is the fault of the unestablished reason (*asiddha-hetu*).
When this cognition subsequently takes [the object] as its condition, the perceived object has already perished; how, then, can it be admitted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)?

When the visual and other consciousnesses perceive form and so forth, they are actually unable to produce such a conceptual determination; this is solely because each [consciousness] internally realizes its own objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*).

With that [sensory cognition] as the precursor, the mental consciousness subsequently grasps its determinate characteristics; only through the synthesis and conceptualization of these can a definitive judgment be reached.
Furthermore, at that time, the various cognitions do not arise simultaneously.
If that were the case, when the various objects such as form and the consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness have ceased, how could one subsequently see?
Since the seer does not exist, how could that which is perceived be established?
At this very moment, what is there to hope for?
Since consciousness has ceased, how could there possibly be seeing?
Moreover, it perishes together with the common consciousness of form and other objects.
Therefore, one should know that this [consciousness] cannot see such objects as form and the rest.

When one observes visible forms and so forth by means of the mind that repeatedly examines through the power of that [initial] seeing, how can this be admitted as being a distinct type of sensory direct perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*)?

Furthermore, at that time, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) performs the function of discernment; since it is not commonly accepted as being of the nature of direct perception, and because the [sensory] seeing has ceased along with its concomitants, [the mental consciousness cannot be so classified].
Other masters say:
Because this [consciousness] initially experiences its object and is not defiled by the stains of conceptualization, it necessarily takes external color-form as its real object.
This is also unreasonable because it is unestablished.

For others do not admit that external objects such as form, which are distinct from verbal designations, are what consciousness cognizes; rather, due to the internal occurrence of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), at that very moment, without the arising of conceptual construction, one immediately perceives the various distinctions among the appearances of objects.

He merely admits that such internal conditions exist; these also manifest according to their respective characteristics, depending solely upon consciousness, just as suffering, pleasure, defilement, and so forth are collectively established.

However, to treat external objects such as form and so forth as distinct objects of sensory cognition is merely a false conceptual attachment; it is like [the case of] number, dimension, action, and so on, where one uses this very objection to resolve other doubts.

Regarding matters seen in a dream, after one has awakened from the dream, one reflects upon them; although at that time there was no external object, there is nevertheless a cognition within the higher mind (*adhicitta*).

Direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is likewise so. For this reason, at a later time, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) definitively ascertains that [the cognition] was not non-existent. Furthermore, it is especially untenable to deny the existence of distinct sensory cognitions (*indriyapramāṇa*) regarding their own internal realization (*svasaṃvedana*), because it is accepted that there is direct perception which does not exist apart from self-realization.
However, to claim that external objects are established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is a false superimposition (*samāropa*), which is precisely what is to be refuted.
As previously stated to avoid the fault of non-establishment (*asiddha*), you have failed to understand the terminology; your words are merely empty talk and lack any precision.
He entirely denies the existence of external forms and the like, yet wishes to rely upon them to clarify the existence of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
However, because that which he seeks to establish cannot avoid the faults already refuted, [his position is untenable].

If the mental consciousness had never previously experienced that object, it would be impossible for recollection to arise; therefore, one must certainly admit that the external object was previously experienced.

Because one can perceive objects such as visible forms, the distinct nature of the sense faculties is admitted; however, this does not establish that one can only remember an object that has previously been experienced. Why is this so?
Because there is logical justification:
it has already been explained that although external objects do not exist, visual and other consciousnesses arise by appearing in the likeness of those objects, as previously stated.
Furthermore, as for how recollection arises from this: following this consciousness, it arises as the mental consciousness that discriminates those very signs, in conjunction with mindfulness.
Since mindfulness arises only by apprehending its respective object, that [proposed] definition is untenable.

If that were so, then regarding forms and other objects, because one generates a state of recollection through the definitive cognition of their characteristics by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would follow that they are like pleasure and so forth.

One establishes the mental image upon recollection and apprehends it; one definitively discerns the preceding signs through internal self-realization. Yet this is not a non-apprehension, for it is unlike stones and the like.
When consciousness arises together with its flames and so forth, it likewise cannot produce this recollection.
Therefore, by the power of inference, one must conclude that there must necessarily be a direct experience of objects such as visible forms.
If it were otherwise, the recollection that is admitted would become non-existent.
Furthermore, because the object experienced therein becomes a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is designated as "seeing" in worldly discourse.
If it were the case that [the cognition] regarding form and so forth were of the nature of recollection, as is commonly established, such a fault would indeed exist.

However, for this very reason, it is logically untenable to maintain that one experiences recollection with respect to external objects such as form, because there is a valid argument [to the contrary].
Just as a visual perception could exist apart from its object, so too would recollection; thus, it cannot serve as a valid probans (*sādhana*) because it is not commonly established (*asādhāraṇa*).
Since both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are intended to inform another, they lack entirely the functional capacity to apprehend an object.
The Commentary on the Precious Production of Consciousness-Only, Scroll Four;
The Commentary on the Precious Production of Consciousness-Only, Scroll Five. Also known as the Explanatory Treatise in Accordance with the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.
The Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Great Tang, by Imperial Decree,
translated this treatise,
which states: How can that which does not engage with or interact with objects such as form be designated as "seeing"?
If this difficulty is thus dispelled, there is no need for further elaboration.
Since the essence of this consciousness itself manifests forms and appearances, the object is established even though color-form and the like do not exist.

This has been explained previously; using dreams, hellish realms, and cataracts as illustrative examples, one should extensively set forth the formal arguments (*anumāna*) as appropriate to each case.
Regarding that which arises from this as recollection (*smṛti*): because it manifests without depending on external objects, its own nature can only arise once [the object] has been seen.

Although it lacks real objective referents, recollection coexists with the mental faculty (*manas*). Due to the power of the manifesting consciousness to establish its functional capacity, and by relying on subsequent conditions as a means of attraction in their proper sequence, conceptualization (*vikalpa*) finally arises; at that moment, it is termed "recollection."
How, furthermore, can one know that seeing (*darśana*) and recollection (*smṛti*) differ in their essential natures?

If both this seeing and recollection do not depend on external objects for their existence and are able to produce their own entities, then—given that they have as their nature the appearance of objects—how can one avoid the doubt of error? It is said that the function of the discerning consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*) is seeing; it does not produce a conceptualization of the characteristics of a prior object, but rather there arises the aspect of recollecting, which is the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*).
Taking up the differences in the arrangement of their verbal characteristics, one realizes that these characteristics are not inherently clear, but arise through discrimination.
With perception as the precursor, they are dispatched by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); thus, this very self-nature arises due to others.
I see this as not being the case; for seeing and recollecting are fundamentally distinct categories, it must necessarily be admitted that such a principle holds.

Even if external objects do exist, although both [seeing and remembering] possess objects and their objective conditions are no different, the intrinsic natures of seeing and recollecting are not the same. If there is indeed a divergent path [between them], you should kindly explain it.

Even if one were to posit that what takes a present object as its condition is called "seeing" (*darśana*), while what takes a past object is called "recollection" (*smṛti*), this distinction would still not constitute a partial conceptualization within seeing or recollection merely because the objects differ in their states of existence or non-existence. Since the conditions (*ālambana*) are distinct, these differing characteristics must be explained as arising from the difference in their own essential natures (*svabhāva*). Thus, they are established as distinct characteristics.
If this object is a manifestation of that consciousness, how can it be known with certainty?

Because one has already ascertained and seen the preceding object, the consciousness that arises resembling it is distinct and not forgotten; when grasping that thing, it is designated as being "like" that object, just as one must first ascertain the features of a man before designating him as being "like" a man.

It is not that the cognition of the "semblance-image" (pratibimba) occurs without having previously seen [the object]; however, it is illogical to claim that such a definitive judgment could arise from what was previously seen, because you do not admit the existence of external objects—this too is unreasonable.

Since it is accepted that the characteristics of the understandings arising from those respective self-cognitions of mind and mental factors are distinct, this certainly does not constitute a valid objection against others.
Since you are so skilled in making such distinctions regarding phenomena, I shall pose a brief inquiry:
How, then, can there be simultaneous self-cognition?
Since its existence is not admitted, how could this perception be determinate?
A past event cannot be remembered, because it lacks the nature of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*).
Furthermore, it is not self-evident, because the matter as described contradicts reason.
One should first establish one's own position and only then strike at the opponent; only through such a strategic presentation can victory be achieved.
This implies that mindfulness arises by depending upon an object; thus, it cannot be established as being "unshared" (asādhāraṇa).

Furthermore, one experiences external objects even within dreams, which would allow for the establishment of such dependence. Later, one can simply say that those [objects] were originally non-existent, because it is irrational [to claim otherwise], just as one experiences pleasant things through feelings such as pleasure (*sukha*).

If external objects were inherently existent and capable of being apprehended, yet only a semblance of them appears in confusion, then at that very moment one naturally determines that external objects do not exist, just as a dreamer realizes upon waking that it was not real.
A dreamer perceives what does not exist, and upon waking, realizes it was false.
If one likewise does not apprehend objects during the waking state, then—just as those things were non-existent in the dream—it will be known by the world itself.

However, this is not the case; therefore, we know with certainty that at the time of correct awakening, there is a genuine apprehension of objects such as form, which differs from the consciousness in dreams that lacks functional efficacy.
This also cannot serve as an illustration to establish the sense of experiencing objects such as forms;
for when one who has dreamed is in the midst of a dream, they are unable to realize that the objects are non-existent.

If, through being free from the darkness of sleep, one attains clear wisdom, then according to the various seeds of memory previously perfumed by those respective objects of experience, one recalls the objects perceived during the dream state and brings them to the surface of the mind; only then does the definitive judgment arise that these things do not exist.
Since that is so, this is likewise the case.

Although it is not an external form that can be apprehended, one immediately reverses this to produce a mind that perceives external forms, giving rise to false conceptualization that manifests repeatedly and is repeatedly taken as an object of cognition. This generates the functional capacity inherent in such a nature; through habitual perfuming, it becomes a seed that causes that [mind] to arise again.
Furthermore, in order to further demonstrate that this very perfuming is unreal, subsequent conditions arise to reveal the true meaning.
Because there is a similarity to the state of sleep, it is called "sleep" even during the waking state, for this perfuming constantly follows and pursues one.

Worldly sleep is like ordinary slumber; yet, with nothing but deluded sentiments and a lack of discernment, one perceives objects such as forms and sounds, thereby becoming entangled and subjected to extreme hardship, drifting through the realms of existence and sinking into the ocean of desire.

Because they have not yet correctly attained the severance of habitual perfuming, they are like those in a dream who cannot realize that objects such as forms do not exist; because they have not yet been able to accord with reality regarding what is non-arising, they fail to understand their non-existence and are deceived by these objects as if they were real.

Even if there is wisdom born of hearing and reflection, because it follows the熏習 (vāsanā) of conceptual discrimination, it cannot correctly arise as a direct realization of reality; this is also called deceptive delusion, and at such a time, it is termed "non-awakening" (abodha).

Furthermore, because the seeds of those latencies have been countered by their antidotes, their deep and powerful functioning has been utterly uprooted; since this [wisdom] does not exist in the world prior to its initial arising, it is called supramundane wisdom (*lokottara-jñāna*), for it correctly eliminates all conceptual natures (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
When non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) attains manifestation, it can eliminate the sleep of ignorance through habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), thereby realizing true awakening.

At that time, by taking this non-conceptual wisdom as the cause and through the power of its skillful application (*upāya*), one is certainly able to sever the firm habitual attachments to objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; this is called "purification."
Because it involves the conceptualization of the characteristics of various objects, it is termed "the world.

When that cognition manifests, it is merely consciousness arising through the power of the convergence of conditions according to its respective categories; at that time, it only manifests its own objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) within its own consciousness, yet it falsely clings to these as external objects, thereby acting as the cause for their production.
However, since there is no intrinsic nature (svabhāva) apart from consciousness, objects such as forms and sounds are produced and cognized.

If the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) established here is based on their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and it is claimed that those objects are non-existent because they are not perceived, then the proponent’s reason (*hetu*) would incur the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddha*).

If one says that [the particular] is not known at the time of the cognition of the distinction, this remains unestablished and is similar to the previous case; for it is a tenet accepted by our own school that at the stage of awakening, the objects are fundamentally non-existent.
Since this fault exists, it is logically impossible for such a capacity to establish that its preceding object is something capable of being apprehended.

Alternatively, regarding this fault of non-establishment, one might offer an explanatory gloss; however, just as a cognition that originally does not take an object as its referent cannot logically establish the existence of that non-existent thing, so too [this proposed explanation] should not be established.
One must first know the object before this mind can arise with respect to that thing; thus, it is said to be "non-existent.
If that is so, and one knows for certain that the preceding object exists, how could one subsequently perceive it again and yet say it is non-existent?
To observe that a characteristic exists and then claim it is non-existent is a manifest contradiction.
However, if one provides a comprehensive explanation for how those various schools negate its existence, there is indeed no contradiction.
Just as various non-Buddhist treatises claim that things are eternal and so forth, [they argue that] prior to arising and after ceasing, they are by no means non-existent.
Whether in terms of spatial location or identity—being this and not another—if an object exists without exception, what fault could there be?
If it were thought that "I" will become non-existent at some time, one could not negate it as non-existent simply because it is not understood;
for it is not accepted that knowledge can arise regarding a non-entity. Thus, this is not according to the literal text, which states here that "I" do not exist in relation to form and so forth.
However, in the context of the formation of form and so forth, there is no real self; it is not based on a self.

If that is so, one might argue that while it is perhaps acceptable to say there is no fault regarding the aggregates of form and so forth, how can one avoid the difficulty of saying that consciousness itself lacks a self?

Since a second consciousness is not admitted, one cannot apprehend "I" as non-existent in the locus of another consciousness; furthermore, it is impossible to recollect a subsequent [moment] without having previously experienced the preceding one.

Even if such a thought were to arise, the object would have already ceased to exist; therefore, one must admit that it is merely consciousness alone that manifests as an appearance, just as you yourself accept.
Thus, within the state of consciousness, one knows "I am non-existent," thereby negating the self; when consciousness arises, this wisdom at that moment knows the essence of non-self.

Nevertheless, by departing from the object and realizing that there is only consciousness, when an object arises as a corresponding appearance, one understands the object to be non-existent; is this not then the same conclusion?

However, when one realizes the absence of self in form and so forth, that [absence] is a universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) regarding form and the like, not a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because each [basis] is taken as having a fixed nature, and their own-essences (*svabhāva*) are distinct.

However, it is not that a semblance possessing a real entity as its characteristic exists; rather, in order to effect a distinction from others, there arises a dissimilar characteristic associated with consciousness. Just as a collection of mental factors exists as a real entity, this [characteristic] manifests and arises within the very essence of consciousness, whereby conventional discourse is thereby produced.
To realize that external objects are merely the perceptions arising from one's own mind and do not inherently exist externally is the nature attained through the most excellent cultivation.

This arises because wisdom is shrouded by the veil of ignorance; thus, when one observes these common characteristics as they appear externally, they are established according to what is seen through worldly convention. Following the sentiments of the world, they are made intelligible through the pathways of verbal expression. Within various treatises, they function as if they were real entities and are explained by means of distinct formal characteristics, while other things are excluded.

In this matter, there ought to be a distinct constituent part; if the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) were real, it would be a universal characteristic in its own right, and like the intrinsic natures of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, each would be distinct. Consequently, it could not be associated with the individual entities [of those things], whereby form and the others would fail to be non-distinct in essence, becoming like form appearing as sound.

Furthermore, just as that common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) which is neither identical nor different is not admitted by verbal expression and merely conceals the conventional, it nevertheless appears clearly to the mind without dispute.
Since this is not admitted to be a real entity, it follows that form, sound, and so forth do not constitute distinct entities.

Furthermore, since each [element] such as form would then possess multiple entities, and since the nature of their common characteristics is infinite, this would result in a combination of many types of essential natures; consequently, all phenomena would become a single entity.

Just as one apprehends the images carried by their respective conditions, this essential nature that demarcates the preceding object is likewise a manifold set of provisional characteristics, conceptually distinguished for the sake of conventional discourse.
Consequently, the wisdom that realizes the selflessness of form, sound, and so forth is also a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because it functions by means of exclusion (*apoha*).
By apprehending their lack of objective referents, this further clarifies the tenet of Consciousness-Only (*vijñapti-mātra*).

However, when there is the understanding of selflessness regarding form and so forth, there is a distinct objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*); furthermore, because this [aspect] is originally non-existent through its preceding and succeeding segments, it constitutes the prior grasping of a distinct aspect with clear decisiveness, whereby one subsequently apprehends the nature of the objective sphere (*vastu-viṣaya*) through that very discernment.
If one were to set aside the white [petals] of a blue lotus, the consciousness would take the body of the lotus as its object and definitively judge it to be blue.
The principle is exactly the same regarding the statement "there is no self.

Whenever a definitive judgment arises, it refers precisely to the characteristic of a self as grasped by others; it is by relying on this mental construction that the judgment "there is no separate entity of a self" is produced.
Even if there were no external objects and cognition could still arise, since the underlying principle is equal and balanced, how could there be any contradiction or dispute?

If it is held that sentient beings [act] through their own continuums, one might say that within these individual substantial bodies there are each infinite and distinct capacities; because they manifest differently within their own consciousnesses, this occurs until the time of maturation.
Consciousness manifests through the power of its own seeds and does not arise by means of external objects; it is not produced from external objects apart from its own consciousness.
However, the claim that benefit and harm occur due to associating with virtuous or non-virtuous friends cannot be established [on such a basis].
Because within the context of the true and the false, or benefit and harm, one merely takes vocal sounds as the object of discourse;
since both the sound and its meaning are non-existent when taken as conditions, the resulting judgment becomes non-existent as well.
Because they possess both rational and irrational modes of conduct, it is possible for good and evil to follow them accordingly.
Since such conduct no longer exists [in that state], how could it be permissible for one to adopt and follow their example? It would certainly not be so.
This would mean that consciousness arises without ever depending upon external objects, which contradicts your own tenet.

Consciousness must necessarily depend upon external objects such as form (*rūpa*) and take such objects as its conditions; it is like a cognition of an existing thing, rather than a cognition of a non-existent sound.
Furthermore, just as one observes the tracks left by others, these are capable of definitively determining objects;

likewise, just as the various cognitions of form and so forth necessarily take external objects as their conditions, yet—as stated in the authoritative words of the Noble Ones—these merely manifest as appearances resembling [objects] within, this [argument] certainly lacks the power to refute the doctrine of Consciousness-Only.

Regarding the phrase "the mutual determination of consciousnesses is established through successive predominance": because the characteristics of these successive consciousnesses are mutually dependent, these two consciousnesses rely upon one another; fundamentally, they do not depend on sound, visible forms, or other such objects.
Since the examples established do not contradict the thesis, there is likewise no fault of contravening the scriptures.

Because there exist other continuums as distinct cognitions, and because one's own cognition arises with the cognition of another as its cause, the principle of the functional efficacy of both virtuous and non-virtuous companions is established.

If external objects are refuted by claiming they are like dreams and thus non-existent, why not apply the same logic to the friend you see with your own eyes? Why do you not dismiss him as unreal while you sleep, instead of laboriously establishing a complex chain of mutually dependent phenomena?
Since hearing of good or evil in a dream does not arise from a separate consciousness, how can it be that [the dreamer] currently acts in accordance with another's consciousness?
Furthermore, how is it known that this arises solely through the discrimination of other consciousnesses?

When one responds to the words and matters of others according to their intent, at the moment this consciousness arises, there is yet another distinct functional capacity of consciousness that serves as the cause for its manifestation.

For instance, regarding the consciousness of a listener: just as when making a pact, it is only through the appearance of the sound that a distinct entity manifests, whereby consciousness is able to arise; it is not by depending on an external object that one can comprehend the matter.
Relying on its own functional capacity, all distinctions are understood as the characteristic of sound by depending upon internal conditions; thus, there is cognition of the object before one.

At this time, it is merely the transformation and arising of the functional capacity of one's own consciousness at its stage of maturation; there is only the characteristic of sound arising simultaneously with the common consciousness. Examine this principle in detail.

Furthermore, the majestic power of the Noble One is supreme; it is devoid of words and transcends the grasping of phonetic characteristics, yet it serves as a skillful means for discourse during intervals of silence.

Thus, it is solely through this superior differentiation that such an act can be performed, subsequently causing other consciousnesses to arise with distinct characteristics. Since this is universally acknowledged, it constitutes the very efficacy of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
In that case, it is commonly accepted by others that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound never reaches other cognitions; this is what is intended as the analogy.
Even if one were to grant this, since the perception of sound would arise based solely on another cognition, it would follow that hearing is constant.
This cognition of sound arises universally; even if one resides at a great distance or one’s faculty of hearing is impaired, one should still hear the speech without any lapse of time.

If you grant that this cognition arises from an external sound, yet at times the auditory consciousness must first function for it to be heard, then the cause of discrimination must still be present, and the corresponding faculty of hearing must likewise be undamaged, before one can discern whether an object is right or wrong.
Consequently, this would result in the fallacy that all [objects] are simultaneously perceived as a single totality.
It is not merely this; for consciousness depends upon the capacity for differentiation.

The determination of an object occurs through sound, just as the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of each sound is distinct; it is the specific characteristic that gives rise to this cognition, and not any other mental state.

It is also like the case of sound, where one does not hear everything; rather, by taking this characteristic of sound as an object, one merely turns back toward it and gives rise only to this specific cognition.
When such a cognition occurs, it arises solely from these particular conditions because they possess functional efficacy; thus, they alone serve as its cause, and nothing else.
Just as with sound, which exists in a corresponding location, it produces a semblance within its own continuum;
furthermore, when the seeds of such a thing manifest, they are able to arise only by following their respective functional fruits, and thus there is no fault of dissimilarity.

Furthermore, all syllables possess constituent parts; when analyzed to their ultimate limit, they are not of a nature perceivable by the sense faculties, just as atoms do not arise simultaneously because they do not aggregate together.
Since they do not aggregate together, the claim that there exists a determinate, permanent sound situated in space is unreasonable; for a mind that perceives such a sound cannot be found.

Furthermore, they maintain that because the nature of its constituent parts is similar, and because it is not an object accessible to the sense faculties, there is no difference in its functional capacity; nor is there any logical principle for the existence of a potentiality for arrangement through its own activity.

Furthermore, just as external sounds produce various echoes according to their respective bases and conditions, and possess their own specific characteristics that serve as the causes for further conditions, so too it is with consciousness; how could it not be desirable?

Is it not the case that what is called "increasingly predominant through successive transmission" implies the admission that this consciousness apprehends other consciousnesses? If so, this consciousness would then possess an external object.
If it did not apprehend an object, the analogy would be contradicted.

This objection is irrational, because this consciousness takes the manifested appearance of other consciousnesses as its object; thus, the analogy is established in common with the positions of other schools.

Just as in those [other] systems, even for a sound that is not presently existing, it is established by means of a single appearance; there is merely the arising of a consciousness of that appearance, and the tenet is thereby admitted as proven.
My analogy is likewise; how could it incur any fault?
For what reason do the distinct consciousnesses of the Tathāgata, having simultaneously eliminated other objects of discrimination, continue to evolve without differentiation?

When sentient beings to be converted, who possess infinite distinctions, have many minds therein, if their mental images were to arise [as distinct], it would be like a single sound whose essence has no difference, yet from which cognitions arise according to the images desired by each individual.
It arises solely through the power of the Tathāgata’s majestic spiritual authority (*anubhāva*) brought to perfection by supreme cultivation, enabling it to manifest.

Regarding various objects of diverse functions that are not of a single kind, yet are numerous and unmixed, their distinct activities are simultaneously accomplished, just as images appear in a lamp, a jewel, or a mirror.

Furthermore, because the various transformative activities of the Tathāgata involve inconceivable power that transcends the realm of discursive thought, and because these are common to [other] systems of study, to raise such an objection is merely a forced argument and does not constitute a profound teaching.

If it is said that the two states of dreaming and waking are not different, this is because both are admitted to lack the nature of real objects; yet, according to their respective distinctions, they all produce effects.
"What is seen in a dream, whether good or evil" is the general heading.
Furthermore, during the state of awakening, the mind likewise lacks objects; consequently, it should also obtain its results simultaneously [with the dream].
Alternatively, like a dream, it should be entirely without results, because of the absence of objective referents.
Alternatively, this objection is not valid because there is a logical reason.

As for the claim that the results of dreaming and waking differ because the mind is impaired by sleep: if that were so, then since the dreaming mind is impaired by sleep and its nature is consequently indistinct, it follows that even wholesome or unwholesome actions performed therein would only be able to produce inferior results.

Just as during the waking state, if one gives a gift while focusing on other matters without reverence, or at times with a mind distracted by other thoughts, although the act of giving is performed, its fruit does not increase.
Although consciousness lacks an external object, the result is likewise the same: according to the distinctions among seeds, it can summon future results—whether desirable or undesirable things.
Therefore, while there is a difference between the substance of dreaming and waking, resulting in different outcomes, this does not contradict the principles of reality.

Furthermore, it is not because of a difference in the intrinsic nature of the objects—such as being wholesome and so forth—that the actions performed bring about superior or inferior results; rather, this occurs due to the increase of the self-substance through its own nature, its association [with other factors], and so on, as well as through their opposition. This is precisely how distinctions exist in dreams and the like.
With this as the condition, it is not related to the existence of an external object.

Sometimes, once [the mind] has arisen, one can give rise to a harmful intent toward that very object and commit an extreme evil; yet, in that same place, one can also attract superior retribution by planting wholesome, middling, or inferior wholesome or unwholesome karmas.
Speaking from this perspective, it is indeed not the case that the diversity of planted fruits depends upon the existence of external objects.

At times, there may be conditions involving such things as the merit of an Arhat’s body in the past; yet, since such objects do not actually exist, the resulting fruits differ just as they do in dreams. Thus, there is the fallacy of non-universality (*anaikāntika*).

Later, while dreaming, he was filled with sincere devotion and joy; yet, although the Tathāgata’s appearance in the world lacks a real objective basis, it still brings about great results. Thus, this analogy fails to accord with his own thesis.
Other masters say:

Although it is impaired by a dream, the mental faculty, though severed from the preceding object, is not darkened; this is like the lingering drowsiness immediately after waking from sleep, or the visual impairment when one is forced to rise before having slept enough, where the body feels heavy and vision is unclear. Such an impairment could certainly not exist within the corresponding consciousness during that dream.

Because at the time when the mind within a dream gives rise to mental phenomena, one clearly perceives the objects of experience with a mind of intense anxiety, fear, and reflection; even during the waking state, one cannot match this.
For this reason, it must necessarily involve a sentient being, because one perceives the aspect of the sign (*nimitta-bhāga*) within a common object of perception.

However, the seven types of material karma (*rūpa-karman*) in a dream do not constitute courses of action (*karmapatha*), because the colors in a dream are not perceived as having resistance (*sapratigha*); they are not common objects of experience and are incapable of serving as the basis for worldly discourse. To claim that such material karma does not constitute a course of action is, therefore, a failure to examine the underlying principles.
However, regarding this discussion: since the vision in that dream-consciousness is not clear, the fruit obtained is slight and inferior; the state of being awake should likewise be so.
Since there is this fault, one might then reply:
"The fruit obtained is small because of the impairment caused by the dream; if it were not impaired, how would it differ from the waking state?"
As it has been said: if dream-consciousness perceives an object with such clarity that it brings about a superior result, how is this to be explained?
It is because within the dream the mind is clear and makes definitive distinctions; thus, it is admitted that such a state can bring about a sublime and excellent retribution.

Regarding why the seven paths of virtuous action (*śukla-karmapatha*) are not established [in this context]: the original purpose was to evaluate the distinctions in the ripening of results (*phala-vipāka*), and thus the paths of action were discussed.

From what source does this line of inquiry derive? It is because the ripening of results does not necessarily depend upon these paths of action for their completion. Rather, it is when one is afflicted by extremely heavy fetters (*paryavasthāna*) during the stage of preliminary application (*prayoga*) that the underlying intention (*āśaya*) is so harmed as to bring about the most evil result. Even if one commits the fundamental act (*maula-karma-patha*), it cannot be the same if the afflictions (*kleśa*) are slight.
It should be understood that this applies analogously to the fact that an extremely pure mind serves as the basis for the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) in the stage of cultivating virtue.

Likewise, according to the Vijñaptimātra theorists, even when harm is inflicted upon the mental continuum of another, the path of action (*karmapatha*) is produced in accordance with the mental factors (*caitta*) that arise.
Other masters say:
"An offense is established only when it is known by another.
This is not a correct answer.
For what reason must one necessarily wait for a common object (*sādhāraṇa-viṣaya*) before establishing this?

It is not that the path of action (*karmapatha*) is first accomplished through the power of another; rather, it relies on that which is fit to be the subject of worldly discourse. For example, when a bhikṣu cuts green plants or discharges filth, how could such offenses depend merely on the state of his own mind? Furthermore, they depend on a common object because they require the knowledge of others.
If, in a dream, there were actually blue and so forth as the objects of cognition, then by the Master’s prohibition, they would indeed constitute an offense.
Other factors may be reversed, but this [case] is logically established not by whether the object exists or does not exist.
If the realm of sentient beings consists solely of consciousness, does it follow that there is no such thing as vocal or bodily action?
However, it is by virtue of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which arises from those elements that what is called "body" exists.
Vocal karma is precisely matter produced from seeds; these two [vocal karma and its seeds] act in concert to accomplish acts such as killing and lying.
If these two types were non-existent, the deed would likewise not exist.
Since hunters and the like incur the sin of killing merely through the manifestation of their own consciousness undergoing transformation, would this not be contradictory?
Is it because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of the preceding life does not terminate by itself that another person incurs the offense of killing?
This contradicts your own tenet regarding the two types of action—bodily and vocal; if not so, how can it be explained?

Regarding death through the consciousness of another: just as in the case of a butcher or a slaughterer, who, having applied the necessary means, causes separation [of life], so too it is here; merely by the fact that one's own consciousness manifests a specific functional differentiation, it becomes the cause for the destruction of that other's life.
Thus, it is merely through the power of one's own consciousness that false bodily forms manifest; by virtue of this momentum, they are established as courses of action (*karmapatha*).
All other courses of action should be understood accordingly.
By this principle, there is furthermore a commonly accepted distinction among consciousnesses that serves as the cause for the destruction of another's body.

This is just as when spirits, *pretas*, *gandharvas*, and the like give rise to malevolent thoughts toward objects they loathe; with the transformation of the consciousnesses of these spirits acting as the cause, it subsequently causes those beings to lose their mindfulness and other faculties from previous lives.

Furthermore, when the noble one focuses his mind in mindfulness, through the superior condition of another's cognitive power, he subsequently dispels the obscurity of sleep within a dream and clearly perceives their various distinct forms and appearances, cognizing and apprehending these manifold images.

Regarding the term "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*): it refers to the limit of time for the stream of the resultant consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that has been projected by the power of karma corresponding to a particular realm of existence. Just as the matter thus projected undergoes transformation, it causes the continuity of the homogeneous maturation (*nikāyasabhāga*) projected by that single karma to be severed; however, this does not mean that all streams [of consciousness] are entirely cut off.

As others maintain, regarding the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), it is said to be "severed" based on the interruption of the homogeneous class (*sabhāga*); it is metaphorically called "severed" when consciousness (*vijñāna*) departs from life.
However, it is solely through the cessation of the activity of both one's own and another's consciousness as conditions that the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is severed.

Just as a hermit attains a supreme meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because the various functional capacities arising from the power of that activity consist merely of internal mental transformations, so too—even in the absence of physical and vocal actions—the principles governing acts such as killing and stealing are perfectly established.
In that sūtra, it is definitively stated that the ascetic, having ignited the fire of anger within his mind, killed immeasurable sentient beings at will by the power of that [anger].

Since this too was brought about by the mind causing their death, one must necessarily infer it according to the same principle as before; one must certainly admit that the ascetic’s intention and the power of his malice were fully accomplished, resulting in the termination of the lives of immeasurable beings.
If it were otherwise, the great sin of mental harm arising from such desire would not result in the actual completion of the act;
therefore, we know that citing this as proof establishes that the mental offense is grave.
Furthermore, if a non-human being, knowing one's intention, were to carry out an act of killing at that time, this too would constitute the most serious offense among manifest physical karmas.

Sometimes, without depending on other successions of consciousness, sentient beings encounter harm such as falling rocks, rain of smoke and embers, and so forth; by whose predominant power is their life severed?
It is certainly not the case that this consciousness manifests such a sign and then itself undergoes slaughter, for that would entail the fallacy of self-binding contradiction.
This objection is irrational, because it is precisely through the incapacity of this consciousness’s continuum to persist that it conforms to the nature of the severance of life.

It is like the poison of doubt that causes the mind to become confused and agitated; it merely follows along with one's own internal continuum, and because consciousness lacks the power to remain further connected, this is called the severance of life-span.
Nevertheless, it does not constitute a contradiction even if one admits that the appearance of stones and such things occurs.
However, as for the claim that one causes another's life to end by means of a dominant consciousness (*adhipati-vijñāna*), why would that person not die immediately thereafter?
At the time of death, that [killing] no longer exists; since it is not present, how can it constitute an offense?
And how could it serve as the causal nature for the taking of life?
Although you have presented this elegant objection, you should instead be asked in return:
Regarding the path of action (*karmapatha*) summoned when one commits killing: if that path of action were completed at the very moment [of the act], why does the victim not die immediately?
If, on the other hand, the path of action is only completed when the victim actually dies due to the conditions [of the act], how can this person be guilty of the transgression of taking life?
If it is claimed that the act of killing occurs through their conjunction, how could these two—which exist at different times and possess distinct natures—perform a single joint action?

Regarding this matter, the Venerable Author of the Treatise has already established a definitive conclusion: within the personal continuum of the perpetrator, there exists a specific nature of karma that flows forth.

However, regarding this matter, I hold such a view: it is due to the predominant consciousness of the killer that the continuity [of the victim] is severed; these [factors] act as mutual causes, and it is determined by this alone, without requiring any other separate entity, that death subsequently occurs.
At the moment one is wounded, the karma of killing is established, for there is efficacy in the taking of another's life, and it is determined by this very act that one undergoes death.

However, that which is capable of killing possesses this power: it acts as the immediate cause for the severing of life, whether death occurs instantly or at a later time. This is because the dominant consciousness (*adhipati-vijñāna*) can act as a successive cause of harm to another consciousness, creating an obstruction for the subsequent moment of the other's consciousness so that it no longer continues.

Nor is it that one who does not physically harm another can still incur the karma of killing merely through the mind; for by this, there is the possibility of retrogression, since the act of inflicting harm upon that being has been abandoned.
Speaking in terms of principle, since the other person does not die by means of any further conditions, they will certainly meet their end through this [act].
Because life is severed by taking this as the cause, the path of action of killing is thereby established; thus, there is no fault in this.
In this way, one should understand the cases of thieves and the like according to their specific circumstances.
If it were otherwise, what power or function would the perpetrator possess at a later time such that they would incur the sin of killing only when the other person has already died?
Furthermore, this would allow for the error of overstepping reason:

it would not depend on the capacity to harm within one's own person having distinctions, but would instead rely solely on the fact that the victim's body possesses specific differences such that the offense is only completed at the time of the subsequent death, because it was through the application of effort that the victim's life was severed.

This has already been addressed by the question, "Why does one not die at that very moment? It should be understood that through the karmic action of killing committed at that time by means of the appropriate expedient, the sin of taking life is incurred immediately; death occurs because of that [karma].
However, since no distinct characteristic can be apprehended at a later time, this same principle must be used to dispel further doubts.

In that case, it would be just like the victim and the perpetrator within a dream; because the body and so forth do not exist [there], this would result in the fault that there are no paths of action (karmapatha).
This is because consciousness within a dream cannot harm the continuum of another; therefore, no course of action (karmapatha) is established therein.
Conversely, when one is awake, such an act does constitute a course of action.
Having already extensively established that it is mind alone which, through uninterrupted activity within the interim, is capable of accomplishing the act of harming—
setting aside for a moment such extensive presentations of divergent views— one must still adhere to the underlying principle and further interrogate these specific points.
If there is only consciousness, does that knowledge of another's mind (paracittajñāna) know the other's mind, or does it not?
If you say it does not know, how can it be said to "know" the other's mind?

This name [of "knowing another's mind"] exists because one knows another's mind through cognition; if one did not know it as it is, it would constitute deception and falsehood, whereby the expressive term itself would be at fault.
If, however, one were to know it as such, then because one would be apprehending an object external to consciousness, the principle of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only) would be contradicted.
Since these two matters are contradictory, how can the objection be resolved?
Why is this so? Because there is a profound meaning [to be understood].

Regarding the question of how the knowledge of others' minds knows its object as it truly is not: this refers to the extremely profound sphere of realization and experience, which is termed "the mind of another.
If one were to allow that [this knowledge] is consciousness (*vijñāna*), it would contradict the nature of knowing another's mind.
If it were non-existent, it would truly contradict your own teaching.

If the knowledge of others' minds were to take external objects as its condition—just as one observes that there are objects external to the mind as conditions—then this difficulty regarding the fault would be unavoidable.

Since the object is understood to be unreal, there is certainly no fault; however, how can it be known that the object does not correspond to its reality, yet still be termed "knowledge of others' minds"?
The meaning here is this: just as the previously perceived object is not false, it is by virtue of this that it is termed "knowledge of others' minds."
If one knows that the preceding object is not as it truly is, how can this be called "knowing the minds of others"?
Such reasoning is incorrect; you have not yet grasped the original intent.

Although the mind of another is not taken as an object, does a representation resembling its appearance manifest upon one's own consciousness? Therefore, while no object exists apart from the mind that can give rise to such a resemblance, it is nonetheless not identical to the actual object; thus, the original intention for establishing "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna) is fulfilled.
In this context, it is merely the apprehension of that which resembles the [external] object; for this reason, it is called "unreality" (*ayathārthatā*).
Although it is not identical to that [object], it arises as something resembling it, because it has already been established through common consensus that there is no object apart from the mind.
That which is capable of knowing arises in accordance with the appearance of objects; it is like knowing one's own mind, for two cognitions cannot coexist simultaneously in a wise person.

Therefore, it is certainly not present; one must admit that it has either already ceased or not yet arisen, such that only one [moment] can be apprehended as its object, and its substance is further non-existent.

It is simply that one's own consciousness takes as its object the mental aggregates of the past and present; this is universally accepted by the world as the manifestation of characteristics through the reception of one's own mind. One should also understand that the principle for cognizing the minds of others is likewise the same.
If one is able to personally discern one's own mind, how can it be said that one does not know it as it truly is?
Is it called "unreal" because of a lack of true knowledge regarding the object?
Is it that by taking what is non-existent to be existent, one is said to have "knowledge according to reality"?
If so, how can it be said that such knowledge does not correspond to its object?
For all that is experienced is non-existent, because it fails to apprehend the actual object.
This is also not the case.

For one who does not know the realm as it is for a Buddha, this knowledge of others' minds perceives the objects of others—such as blue and so forth—and that very perception of those objects is what constitutes knowing reality as it is.
How can one claim not to know the Buddha’s knowledge of the nature of the mind, which is inherently pure by its very essence?

Generally speaking, when one is said to "know another's mind," it is by taking that other's mind as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) to realize the characteristics of one's own mind; this is merely a conventional designation for "knowing another. What, then, is the true, essential reality of that other's mind? It is the state of ultimate reality (*tathatā*).
This is also not the case. Why is that?
Because the Buddha knows the intrinsic nature of another's mind; that is, he knows its existence by means of a cognition that is itself free from [the object of] mind.
If there were form existing apart from the mind, what harm would it do for the Buddha to perceive it?
This [position] that the mind is substantially existent is established as being mutually accepted by both parties.
However, form that exists substantially apart from the mind contradicts reason; therefore, the two cases are not the same.
If that were so, the Buddha’s knowledge of others’ minds would not be knowledge of the actual object, because the object is illusory.
What harm is there, moreover, in the Buddha relying upon such illusory knowledge?
It is like a person observing a magical illusion; how could they not know it to be empty?
The Buddha’s knowledge is identical to emptiness; what fault could there be?
If this is so, what characteristics does the realm of the Buddhas possess?
The realm of the Buddhas is not something known by others.
If the Buddha did not know the mind, how could he be called "Omniscient"?
It is precisely when that unerring intrinsic nature has its sleep of ignorance exhausted, attaining clear awakening and perfect understanding.
Those who claim to perceive the minds of themselves and others cannot actually perceive their true nature; therefore, it is said that such cognition does not accord with the knowledge of the object.
Furthermore, how can one reconcile this with the claim that the wisdom of one whose sleep has been exhausted can correctly perceive this?
By means of this, one realizes the nature of the ineffable realm, which transcends the path of speech and is known only through self-realization; therefore, it cannot be reached by verbal expression.
Nevertheless, the intrinsic nature of this consciousness cannot be known by any other consciousness.

Since it is neither an object of knowledge nor can it be reached by speech—because that [object] takes only the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its domain—it consists solely of the nature of false conceptual construction (*parikalpita*).

This very conceptual construction, in relation to the nature of self-realization (*svasaṃvedana*), is extremely remote from the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of consciousness. Thus, within the sphere of consciousness, one realizes only the unreality of these two; both become objects that do not correspond to reality.
Why is this so? Because one forms a determination based on the understanding that unreal things are real, due to the manifestation of false appearances within that consciousness.
*Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-ratnasambhava-śāstra*, Fascicle Five.
